hints: Recall the definition linked to Newton's second law in terms of momentum rather than only mass and acceleration.
teacher_walkthrough: Force is defined by the rate of change of momentum of a body.
In symbols: $$F = \frac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}$$ where $F$ is the resultant force and $\Delta p$ is the change in momentum in time $\Delta t$.
walkthrough: B1: state force is rate of change of momentum.
common_pitfalls: Giving a vague statement such as a push or a pull without the momentum rate definition does not gain credit.
Stating $F = ma$ alone is insufficient because the syllabus definition required here is in terms of momentum.

hints: Read the value of $X$ from Fig. 3.2 between $t = 0$ and $t = 3.0\,\text{s}$ and subtract the constant resistive force to get the resultant force.
Use impulse equals change in momentum: $\Delta p = F_{net} \times \Delta t$ with $\Delta t = 3.0\,\text{s}$.
teacher_walkthrough: Impulse of the resultant force equals change in momentum: $$\Delta p = F_{net} \Delta t$$
From Fig. 3.2, $X = 1.4\,\text{N}$ for $0$ to $3.0\,\text{s}$. Resistive force $f = 0.80\,\text{N}$ opposite to motion.
Resultant force: $$F_{net} = X - f = 1.4 - 0.80 = 0.60\,\text{N}$$
Time interval: $$\Delta t = 3.0 - 0 = 3.0\,\text{s}$$
Change in momentum: $$\Delta p = 0.60 \times 3.0 = 1.8\,\text{kg}\,\text{m}\,\text{s}^{-1}$$
walkthrough: C1: calculate resultant force times time as $(1.4 - 0.80) \times 3.0$.
common_pitfalls: Using $X = 1.4\,\text{N}$ directly as the resultant force and omitting the $0.80\,\text{N}$ resistance.
Misreading Fig. 3.2 as $X = 1.0\,\text{N}$ or using the later $0.80\,\text{N}$ value of $X$.

hints: Read the new value of $X$ from Fig. 3.2 for $t = 3.0\,\text{s}$ to $t = 6.0\,\text{s}$ and compare it with the $0.80\,\text{N}$ resistive force.
Apply Newton's first law: consider what zero resultant force implies for acceleration and velocity.
teacher_walkthrough: Newton's first law relates resultant force to motion: $$F_{net} = ma$$ so zero $F_{net}$ gives zero acceleration.
From Fig. 3.2, for $3.0\,\text{s}$ to $6.0\,\text{s}$: $$X = 0.80\,\text{N}$$
Resultant force: $$F_{net} = X - f = 0.80 - 0.80 = 0\,\text{N}$$
Since $F_{net} = 0$, acceleration $a = 0$. The block continues with the velocity it had at $3.0\,\text{s}$, so it moves with constant velocity.
walkthrough: B1: resultant force is zero because $X$ equals resistive force.
B1: moves with constant velocity / zero acceleration.
common_pitfalls: Stating the block stops because forces are balanced, ignoring that it already has velocity from the earlier acceleration.
Stating only that forces are equal without linking zero resultant force to constant velocity.

hints: Start from power as rate of doing work: $P = W/t$ gives work done by force $X$ over the $3.0\,\text{s}$ interval.
Recall work done by a constant force in its direction of motion is $W = Fs$, where $F$ is force $X$ itself.
Combine to get $s = Pt/F$ and check that $F = 0.80\,\text{N}$ is the force doing the stated power, not the resultant force.
teacher_walkthrough: Power is the rate of work done: $$P = \frac{W}{t}$$ so $$W = Pt$$
Time interval: $$\Delta t = 6.0 - 3.0 = 3.0\,\text{s}$$
Work done by $X$: $$W = 2.0 \times 3.0 = 6.0\,\text{J}$$
Work by constant force $X$ in direction of motion: $$W = Fs$$ where $F = X = 0.80\,\text{N}$.
Distance: $$s = \frac{W}{F} = \frac{6.0}{0.80} = 7.5\,\text{m}$$
walkthrough: C1: use work done $= Fs$ to get $s = W/F$.
common_pitfalls: Using the resultant force of zero in $W = Fs$, which would incorrectly give zero work or undefined distance.
Using the wrong time, such as $6.0\,\text{s}$ instead of the interval $3.0\,\text{s}$, when calculating $W = Pt$.

hints: Use the link between resultant force and gradient of a momentum-time graph: constant non-zero $F_{net}$ from $0$ to $3.0\,\text{s}$ means a constant gradient starting from zero.
Consider what zero resultant force after $3.0\,\text{s}$ means for momentum, and ensure there is no sudden jump at $t = 3.0\,\text{s}$.
teacher_walkthrough: Gradient of momentum-time graph equals resultant force: $$F_{net} = \frac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}$$
From $t = 0$ to $t = 3.0\,\text{s}$, $F_{net} = 0.60\,\text{N}$ constant and block starts from rest ($p = 0$ at $t = 0$). So momentum rises linearly from the origin with constant positive gradient.
From $t = 3.0\,\text{s}$ to $t = 6.0\,\text{s}$, $F_{net} = 0$, so $\Delta p = 0$. Momentum stays constant at the value reached at $3.0\,\text{s}$.
Sketch: straight rising line from $(0,0)$ to $t = 3.0\,\text{s}$, then horizontal line to $t = 6.0\,\text{s}$ with a smooth join and no vertical step.
walkthrough: B1: rising straight line from the origin for $0$ to $3.0\,\text{s}$.
B1: horizontal line at non-zero momentum after $3.0\,\text{s}$ with no step change at $3.0\,\text{s}$.
common_pitfalls: Drawing a step down at $3.0\,\text{s}$ because $X$ drops, rather than a change in gradient only.
Drawing momentum falling to zero or rising further after $3.0\,\text{s}$ instead of a horizontal constant-momentum line.
